# async-agent-message-bus An asynchronous multi-agent simulation engine where concurrent LLM agents communicate through a structured message-passing bus — demonstrated on a hybrid-threat (disinformation + infrastructure disruption) tabletop scenario. Built as part of my portfolio for research in AI-driven social simulations. It directly implements three ideas from that field: **structured message-passing protocols**, **dozens of concurrent LLM instances**, and **hybrid-threat scenario simulation**. ## Architecture ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph Agents [Concurrent async agents] G[Government] M[Media] O[Grid Operator] A[Adversary
disguised as citizen] C[Citizen population
n = config parameter] end B[(MessageBus
asyncio.Queue per agent)] G <--> B M <--> B O <--> B A <--> B C <--> B B --> T[JSON transcripts
results/] T --> AN[analyse.py
two-lexicon metrics + charts] ``` - **Structured protocol** — every message is a validated Pydantic model with a typed `MsgType` (BROADCAST / DIRECT / PROPOSAL / ALERT), sender, recipient, round and timestamp. - **True concurrency** — each agent is an asyncio task; LLM calls run via `asyncio.to_thread` behind a semaphore that rate-limits concurrent inference (2 on an 8 GB MacBook Air; a config knob at scale). - **Information asymmetry** — each agent holds private knowledge the others lack; the adversary appears on the bus under a false identity. - **Config-driven scenarios** — roles, private information, round count and population size all live in `scenarios/*.json`. ## The experiment A covert influence agent ("concerned_citizen") tries to spread a false "hidden cyberattack" narrative during a power-grid outage that is, in ground truth, a technical substation fault known only to the operator. Two runs, measured with a two-lexicon keyword analysis (suspicion terms vs. generalised-distrust terms), each per round and per distinct agent: | Run | Agent style | Outcome by round 4 | |-----|-------------|--------------------| | 1 | Operational jargon (persona bleed) | Suspicion terms 3→10 hits; 6/12 agents voicing suspicion | | 2 | Natural public voices | Suspicion dies after round 1 — but distrust terms 6→27; **12/12 agents** in the distrust register | **Headline finding:** the false narrative did not spread in its original form — it *mutated* into a generalised transparency grievance that saturated the entire population, including the truthful actors. A single-lexicon metric reported the narrative as dead; only the two-lexicon measure caught the mutation. Charts for both runs are in `results/`. ## Run it yourself Requires [Ollama](https://ollama.com) with `llama3.2:3b` pulled. ```bash python3 -m venv venv && source venv/bin/activate pip install -r requirements.txt python main.py # run the scenario python analyse.py results/transcript-.json # metrics + chart ``` Tests: `python test_bus.py` (routing), `python test_agents.py` (concurrency). ## Scaling See [HPC_SCALING.md](HPC_SCALING.md) for how this architecture maps onto SLURM/NAISS GPU clusters (agents → array tasks, in-process queue → broker, local Ollama → batched inference serving). ## Honest limitations - The 3B model exhibits **persona drift** under social pressure (in run 1 the adversary was peer-pressured into constructive behaviour) and occasional instruction leakage ("Here's a public post that…"). - Keyword lexicons are a transparent but crude proxy; the natural upgrade is LLM-based stance classification per message. - Ground truth here is scripted; real influence operations are adaptive. ## Ethics note This simulates disinformation *dynamics* at the level of public description — the tabletop-exercise format used in resilience research — to study how false narratives spread and how institutions respond. It contains no operational techniques.
